reading.title: How Filmmakers and Musicians Shape Time
reading.purpose: Explore how the roots chron and temp describe time across history, music, and film.
paras: Whether you are conducting an orchestra or filming a historical drama, managing time is half the craft. In English, two ancient roots—the Greek chron and the Latin temp—give artists exact words for every temporal detail, anything connected to time and sequence. A town historian might write a careful chronicle, a detailed record of events arranged in strict chronological order from the earliest year to the latest.

Film crews have to guard that order closely. Nothing breaks the spell of an 1850s movie faster than an anachronism, an object placed in the wrong era, such as a plastic water bottle resting on a wooden stagecoach seat. Prop designers check every button and lantern so contemporary items from our modern day never sneak into a nineteenth-century scene. Even temporary sets built for just two weeks of shooting must look lived-in for decades.

Musicians think about time in beats rather than centuries. A conductor sets the tempo, the steady speed at which a piece moves from measure to measure, while players watch the baton to synchronize their entrances so every violin and horn lands on the exact same beat. In jazz, a soloist may also deliver an extemporaneous melody, inventing musical phrases on the spot without a written script.

Sometimes time shows up as a stubborn challenge. A chronic problem—one that lingers for years or keeps returning, such as a creaky theater floor—takes patience to fix. From stage props to symphony halls, paying attention to chron and temp helps audiences feel when every moment lands right on cue.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "anachronism" most nearly means
choices: a wooden stagecoach built for a two-week movie shoot
an object or detail placed in the wrong time period
a musical phrase invented on the spot by a jazz player
a careful record of town events written in date order

qs.q: How is a jazz soloist's extemporaneous melody different from a written orchestra part?
choices: The soloist invents the melody on the spot without following a written script.
The soloist plays only contemporary songs written in the nineteenth century.
The soloist ignores the steady speed of the piece and stops every few measures.
The soloist uses a plastic water bottle to keep time with the wooden stage.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 defines extemporaneous directly as "inventing musical phrases on the spot without a written script."

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Historical movies are much harder to make than live jazz concerts or town histories.
Prop designers should avoid building temporary sets because they always look too modern.
Words built from the roots chron and temp describe how historians, filmmakers, and musicians manage time.
Creaky theater floors are the most serious chronic issue facing modern symphony orchestras.
qs.why: The reading connects chron and temp words across history, film production, and music to show how artists control time.
